raw_response:
I will keep my land mostly in the wheat-maize rotation, because here in Quzhou County that is still the steadiest way for me to get grain, use my irrigation water carefully, and avoid taking too much market risk. I already know how to manage wheat and maize well, the local weather and soils fit them, and the work calendar also matches what I can handle. I will put most of my land into winter wheat first and then summer maize on the same fields after wheat harvest. I will keep a smaller piece in spring peanut, because it spreads my risk a little, brings in some cash, and does not need as much nitrogen as grain. I will not chase too many fancy crops this year. At my age, I care more about a stable yield, work I can manage, and avoiding a bad year from trying something uncertain.

For management, I will use improved or hybrid seed instead of old saved seed on the main crops, because I want more even emergence and better resistance. On wheat, I will prepare the field well, use base fertilizer, irrigate at the key stages, and keep weeds and aphids under control with a few timely sprays instead of many random ones. After wheat harvest, I will move quickly into summer maize so I do not lose moisture or planting time. On maize, I will use hybrid seed, place more nitrogen on it than on peanut, and focus irrigation around the sensitive growth stages if rainfall is short. On peanut, I will keep fertilizer moderate, especially nitrogen, because too much vine growth is not what I want. I will use rotary tillage on the peanut field and mainly rotary tillage for the wheat-maize land too, because it saves labor and fits the machinery I would use. My goal this year is not the highest possible yield on paper; it is a reliable, manageable season with steady output.
